pages.name: No square below 0
pages.text: You already know that `3 × 3 = 9`, and from Negative numbers that `−3 × −3 = 9` too, while `0 × 0 = 0`. Every number on the line, times itself, lands at 0 or to the right of it. So the example `x² = −9` has no answer on the line.

pages.name: Squares to −9
pages.task: Which number on the line squares to `−9`?
pages.why: `3 × 3 = 9` and `−3 × −3 = 9`, and every other number on the line squares to 0 or more. So no number on the line squares to `−9`, and we need a new kind of number.

pages.text: Draw each number as an arrow from 0. Times `−1` keeps the arrow's length and points it the other way: it turns it through 180°, a [[half turn]]. Do it twice and the arrow makes a full turn, 360°, back on 1, just as `−1 × −1 = 1`. Tap × −1 to turn it yourself.

pages.name: The quarter turn, j
pages.text:
A quarter turn leaves the arrow from 1 pointing straight up, off the line. No number on the line can do that, so it is a new number, called [[j]]. Times `j` turns an arrow 90° anticlockwise, and two quarter turns make a half turn, so `j × j = −1`. Maths books write `i` for the same number; engineers write `j`, because `i` already means current.
Three quarter turns, 270°, done twice make 540° and land on `−1` too. That arrow points straight down, which is `j` turned half round, `−1 × j`: it is `−j`.
pages.alt: The handle turns the arrow 270 degrees; done twice, 540 degrees, landing on minus 1. j times j: minus 1. minus j times minus j: minus 1.

pages.name: j cubed
pages.task: `j³` is `j × j × j`. Where does it point? Count the quarter turns from 1.
pages.why: Three quarter turns, `3 × 90° = 270°`, leave the arrow pointing straight down. In numbers, `j³ = j² × j = −1 × j = −j`.

pages.name: Two square roots
pages.text:
People call `j` [[the square root of −1]], and in the same way read `√−9` as `j3`, since `(j3)² = −9`. Books differ on which comes first. mathcentre starts from `j = √−1` and gets `j × j = −1` from it; one paper on teaching calls that start unjustifiable, as it leads to misconceptions. This lesson leads with `j × j = −1`.
Here is one muddle. Read `√−4` as `j2`. The usual rule `√a × √b = √(ab)` gives `√36 = 6`, but `j2 × j3 = j × j × 6 = −6`: two quarter turns and a stretch to 6. When both numbers under the roots are negative, write each with `j` first.

pages.name: Back to the quadratic
pages.text:
Back to `x² + 2x + 5 = 0`. Here `a = 1`, `b = 2` and `c = 5`, so `b² − 4ac = 4 − 20 = −16`. That is `(j4)²`, so the formula gives `x = (−2 ± j4) ÷ 2 = −1 ± j2`, the ÷ 2 being `2a`.
An ordinary number plus a `j` part is a [[complex number]], in general `a + jb` (new letters, not the quadratic's). Here `−1` is its [[real part]] and 2 its `j` part, which books call the [[imaginary part]]. That is only a name: later lessons measure the `j` part of a circuit in ohms.
